blocks.text: 1. Xavier Initialization

blocks.alt: Layer size determines a scaled variance, forming Xavier initialization

blocks.text: The scale problem, already covered in genuine depth in the Random Initialization topic, needed a real, mathematically grounded solution. Xavier Initialization is the first genuinely, mathematically principled fix for exactly that problem.

It is named after its own original researcher, Xavier Glorot, and it is sometimes also called Glorot Initialization for exactly this reason, both names referring to the exact same underlying technique covered throughout this topic.
2. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: Xavier init keeps variance stable across layers

blocks.text: This connects back to the scale problem already covered in the Random Initialization topic. Xavier Initialization scales each layer's initial random weights based on that specific layer's own actual size.

More inputs, or more outputs, means genuinely smaller individual weight values get used, a direct, deliberate adjustment specifically designed to keep the overall scale of a layer's output well-behaved, regardless of how large or small that particular layer actually happens to be.
3. The Mathematical Formula

The variance of the initial weights is set based on the number of inputs to that layer, plus the number of outputs from that layer, a specific, genuinely principled formula, rather than an arbitrary, fixed constant applied uniformly everywhere.

This directly addresses the exact limitation already covered in the Random Initialization topic's naive approach, where a fixed scale ignored a layer's own actual size entirely, producing genuinely inconsistent output magnitudes across layers of different sizes.

blocks.text: 4. Preserving Variance Across Layers

blocks.alt: A layer keeps the same variance going in and out

blocks.text: The genuinely core mathematical goal is to keep the variance of activations roughly the same, from layer to layer, as data actually flows forward through the network.

This means activations neither shrink toward zero, nor grow without any limit, as they pass through many stacked layers, directly solving the exact scale problem already covered in the Random Initialization topic, at every single layer throughout the entire network simultaneously.
5. The Connection to Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
This connects back to vanishing and exploding gradients, already covered in full depth in the Backpropagation topic. Xavier Initialization directly targets the exact root cause of both problems.

Poorly scaled values compounding across many layers, right from the very first forward pass, is precisely what Xavier Initialization's own variance-preserving approach, already covered in the previous section, is specifically designed to prevent from ever actually starting.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Preventing a problem before it starts, right at initialization, is genuinely more effective than trying to fix vanishing or exploding gradients after they have already begun compounding across many layers during actual training.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuinely Good Fit for Tanh and Sigmoid

blocks.alt: Xavier init fits tanh and sigmoid well

blocks.text: This connects back to Tanh and Sigmoid, both already covered in the Activation Functions module. Xavier Initialization was originally derived assuming this specific kind of activation function, one with a smooth, symmetric curve centered around zero.

This makes it a genuinely good mathematical fit for these particular activation functions specifically, since the underlying mathematical derivation directly assumes the exact kind of smooth, symmetric behavior Tanh and Sigmoid, both already covered in their own topics, actually exhibit.
7. A Genuine Limitation With ReLU

A genuine, real limitation, discovered through later research, connects back to ReLU, already covered in its own dedicated topic. Xavier's own original derivation does not account for ReLU's own asymmetric behavior, since ReLU treats positive and negative inputs in a genuinely different, non-symmetric way.

This directly motivated He Initialization, the very next topic in this module, a targeted adjustment specifically designed to work well with ReLU and its own variants, already covered throughout the Activation Functions module.
8. Uniform Versus Normal Variants

blocks.alt: A uniform distribution variant is compared against a normal distribution variant

blocks.text: This connects back to the uniform and normal distributions, both already covered in the traditional Machine Learning course. Xavier Initialization can be implemented using either distribution to actually draw the random initial weight values.

Both variants use the exact same core mathematical formula already covered throughout this topic, differing only in the specific shape of the random distribution the actual weight values get drawn from, rather than in the underlying scaling principle itself.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Xavier Initialization Is Genuinely Right

blocks.alt: Using tanh or sigmoid points toward using Xavier initialization

blocks.text: A layer using Tanh or Sigmoid, both already covered in their own dedicated topics, is a genuinely well-matched, mathematically principled fit for Xavier Initialization, exactly the activation functions its original derivation actually assumed.

A layer using ReLU or its own variants instead, all already covered throughout the Activation Functions module, finds He Initialization, covered in the very next topic, the genuinely better-suited choice, given the specific limitation already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Xavier Initialization is the first genuinely, mathematically principled fix for the scale problem.
It scales weights based on a layer's own actual size, its input and output count together.
Its core mathematical goal is preserving activation variance roughly consistently from layer to layer.
It directly targets the root cause of vanishing and exploding gradients, right from the first forward pass.
It was originally derived assuming a smooth, symmetric activation function like Tanh or Sigmoid.
It does not account for ReLU's asymmetric behavior, directly motivating He Initialization, covered next.
It can be implemented using either a uniform or a normal distribution, both scaled by the same core formula.
It genuinely fits layers using Tanh or Sigmoid; ReLU-based layers are better served by He Initialization.
Next up: He Initialization, a targeted adjustment specifically designed to work well with ReLU and its variants.
